files.name: Greeter.java

notes.5: Creates the default interpolator — which, pre-1.10, enabled `script`, `dns`, and `url` lookups.
notes.7: Interpolates the string, expanding any `${...}` the name contains.

options.label: Building the string with `+` is inefficient for long names
options.whyWrong: Performance is irrelevant; the interpolation step is the danger.

options.label: `createInterpolator()` enables lookups (script, url, dns), and the name is interpolated, so `${script:...}` executes code and `${url:...}` makes server-side requests
`replace()` can throw on an unmatched `}`
options.whyWrong: A parse exception is trivial next to code execution.

options.label: Strip '${' from name before interpolating
options.whyWrong: Nested/obfuscated expressions can reconstruct the marker after stripping.

options.label: Don't run untrusted input through an interpolator; insert `name` as data without expression evaluation
Catch exceptions thrown by replace()
options.diff: +    try { return interpolator.replace(...); } catch (Exception e) { return "Hello!"; }
options.whyWrong: The lookup executes during replace(); catching afterward doesn't prevent it.

options.label: HTML-encode name before interpolating
options.whyWrong: Wrong context; HTML escaping doesn't stop `${...}` lookups from firing.

training.exploit: Pass a name of `${script:javascript:java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec('id')}` — the interpolator's script lookup evaluates it and runs the command (remote code execution). `${url:UTF-8:http://169.254.169.254/...}` turns it into SSRF, and `${dns:...}` exfiltrates data over DNS.

hints.line: The RCE is in the interpolation of user text.
hints.bugClass: Attacker text is evaluated as an expression.
hints.why: What lookups does the default interpolator enable?
hints.fix: Never interpolate untrusted input; keep it as data.

writeup.summary: `StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator()` (before Commons Text 1.10) registered `script`, `dns`, and `url` lookups. Interpolating a string that embeds the user's `name` means a value like `${script:javascript:...}` is evaluated as code — remote code execution — while `${url:...}`/`${dns:...}` enable SSRF and exfiltration. This is Text4Shell. The fix is to never run untrusted input through an interpolator: build the greeting with the name as plain data, or use a substitutor configured without the dangerous lookups.
